title: Isaac redigs the wells (Genesis 26:17–22)
hookLine: the quiet patriarch reopens his father's wells and gives them their old names

cards: Of the three fathers of Genesis, Isaac is the quiet one. Abraham gets the journeys and the arguments. Jacob gets the ladder and the wrestling.
Isaac gets a few chapters, and a story about wells. Abraham has died. There's a famine, and Isaac settles among the Philistines, in a place called Gerar.
He plants, and the land gives back a hundredfold. He grows rich, and the neighbors grow jealous. Years before, Abraham's servants had dug wells there.
Now the Philistines have stopped them all up, filled them with dirt. In a dry land, a well is life. Blocking one is a way of saying: you don't belong here.

teach.h: HE DIGS HIS FATHER'S WELLS AGAIN.
teach.b: Isaac doesn't fight. He moves, and he digs. He opens his father's old wells, one by one.
Then, in the old JPS translation: "and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them." He doesn't rename them after himself. Then his servants dig new wells.
At the first, local herdsmen argue: the water is ours. Isaac names it Esek, quarrel, and moves on. At the second, they argue again: Sitnah, enmity.
He moves on. At the third, nobody fights.
He names it Rehoboth, wide spaces, room: "For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land." Some Jewish teachers read this as a picture of every generation.

The wells our parents dug, the practices, the prayers, the Shabbat table, get stopped up over time, forgotten. Each generation has to dig them out again, often honoring them by keeping their old names.
Only then do new wells come. And Isaac adds his own.
One view in the Talmud says each of the fathers began one of the three daily prayers: Abraham the morning, Jacob the evening, and Isaac the afternoon.

teach.h: THE LORD HATH MADE ROOM FOR US.
teach.b: For Isaac, it points to the day he went out to the field at evening to meditate, the day Rebekah first saw him. In that view, the quiet one gave Jews the prayer in the middle of the busy day.
He didn't build anything new and grand. He kept digging until the water came.

how: Jewish tradition sets three daily prayers, and one teaching links the afternoon prayer, Minchah, to Isaac; the story of the wells is read in the Torah portion Toldot.

games.q: you're Isaac. you've dug a new well, and the local herdsmen say, the water is ours. what do you do?
o: name it quarrel and dig somewhere else.
games.why: he names it Esek, quarrel, and moves on; then Sitnah, enmity. at the third well no one fights, and he names it Rehoboth, room.

practice: Think of a good habit you let go, something that once gave you water: a morning walk, a phone call with your grandmother, reading before bed, lighting candles on Friday, a few minutes of quiet.
Picture it filled in with dirt, not by anyone's fault, just by life, then picture the first shovelful: what would that small step be? If you pray, you can ask for the strength to go back.
